results.question: Team ES2005 had a per-unit production cost target from the start of the project. In the final meeting, what did the prototype first come to, what was the target, and how did they get back under budget?
results.gold_answer: The target was 12.50 Euros per unit (half the 25 Euro selling price). In the final meeting the Project Manager (C) said the prototype would cost 14.6 Euros; he suggested flattening the shape, and the Industrial Designer (A) noticed the double-curved case had been entered twice in the cost sheet. Taking out the duplicate brought it to 11.60 Euros, under the 12.50 limit.
results.answer: In the final meeting, Speaker C (Project Manager) reported the prototype's unit cost at 14.60 EUR, against a production cost target of 12.50 EUR set at the kick-off. The team got under budget by removing three costed items, including one of the two double-curved elements that Speaker A (Industrial Designer) had identified as the biggest expense, bringing the cost to 11.60 EUR.

results.question: In ES2005's second meeting the Industrial Designer assumed the remote would run on ordinary batteries. What energy source did the team end up with, which alternatives were rejected, and who argued for the final choice?
results.gold_answer: In meeting b the Industrial Designer (A) suggested just regular batteries. In meeting c A offered a hand dynamo and solar power; the Marketing Expert Raj (B) argued against both and proposed a rechargeable battery, and the Project Manager (C) backed it with a recharging stand. The final prototype in meeting d has a yellow charging stand.
results.answer: Speaker A (Industrial Designer) initially assumed regular batteries as the energy source. The team ultimately chose a rechargeable battery recharged on a base station that doubles as a stand, rejecting a hand-dynamo (users would have to crank it before voice activation) and solar power (unreliable without sunlight). Speaker B (Marketing Expert, Raj) argued for the rechargeable battery, and Speaker C (Project Manager) backed him.

results.question: In ES2012, who first proposed a rechargeable battery or charging dock, who argued for a different power solution instead, and what energy source was confirmed in the third meeting?
results.gold_answer: The Industrial Designer Kate (B) proposed a rechargeable battery or battery dock in meeting b. The Project Manager (A) argued people forget to recharge things and proposed a sealed, long-life battery with no battery compartment, replaced free if it ever ran down. In meeting c the PM confirmed a long-term battery expected to last five to ten years and guaranteed for five years.
results.answer: Speaker B (Industrial Designer, Kate) first proposed a big energy source, "perhaps some sort of rechargeable battery or a battery dock," in the second meeting. Speaker A (Project Manager) argued instead for a disposable remote with a long-lasting battery that would last five to ten years, and the third meeting confirmed a long-term battery source (a sealed long-life battery).

results.question: In IS1000's third meeting the Industrial Designer promised to bring cost figures to the next meeting. What costs were reported for the two prototype designs, and what did the team finally decide given the 12.50 Euro budget?
results.gold_answer: The Industrial Designer Mael promised an exact cost price, and the PM asked for two designs, one less and one more advanced. In the final meeting the basic surfboard-shaped TV remote was put at about 8 Euros and the advanced one (LCD, speech recognition, cover) at 16 Euros, of which speech recognition was about 3 Euros. After recosting with the PM's company price sheet, they cut the LCD and speech recognition and went back to the basic design at about 12 Euros, 50 cents under budget.
results.answer: Speaker C (User Interface Designer) and Speaker D (Industrial Designer) costed the two prototypes at about 8 Euros for the basic, cost-focused design and about 16 Euros for the advanced design with speech recognition and an LCD display. Because the advanced design was over the 12.50 Euro budget, the team dropped speech recognition and the LCD, added two buttons, and settled on the basic design at about 12 Euros, with a plastic case.

results.gold_answer: In meeting b the PM recorded speech recognition as an extra only 'when we have enough money left'. In meeting c he called speech control the unique idea of the remote, and the meeting-d prototype had a microphone. In the final costing the design came to about 18.5 against a 12.50 Euro limit, so the Marketing Expert (D) proposed scrapping the sample speaker and the PM agreed. The team dropped speech recognition (together with the push-scroll wheel) even though the UI Designer (B) objected that it was a special new feature.
results.answer: Before the final meeting, speech recognition was an optional feature: in the second meeting Speaker A (Project Manager) said the team would add it only "if there's enough money" after costs, and in the third meeting Speaker C (Industrial Designer) noted the chip could support it but was still in a test phase. In the fourth meeting, when production cost stood at 18.5 points against the 12.50 EUR limit, the team dropped speech recognition together with the sample speaker, microphone and scroll wheel. The reason was cost: they had to cut points to meet the limit, and speech recognition was the optional, expensive extra that could go.

results.question: In team TS3005's functional design meeting, who argued for an LCD touch screen and with what evidence, who warned it clashed with keeping the remote cheap, and did the LCD survive the final costing?
results.gold_answer: The Marketing Expert (Speaker D) pushed for the LCD, citing survey figures: 81% of 16-25 year olds were interested in an LCD screen, and the target group was 16-45. The Industrial Designer (Speaker C) warned that LCD screens are very expensive and clash with the mission to make it cheap. The PM settled on 'for now it's LCD', with buttons as a backup. In the final meeting the LCD screen was kept, and the scroll wheel and speech recognition were cut instead.
results.answer: Speaker D (Marketing Expert) argued for the LCD touch screen in the second meeting, citing survey data that 81% of 16–25 year olds, 66% of 26–35 and 55% of 36–45 were interested in LCD screens, and that an LCD is easier to keep clean and use than worn rubber buttons. Speaker C (Industrial Designer) warned that an LCD screen, and a touch screen even more so, collides with the mission to make the remote very cheap. The LCD survived the final costing: in the fourth meeting the team cut the speaker, microphone, speech feature, scroll wheel and curve to reach the 12.50 EUR limit, and kept the LCD screen.

results.question: In team TS3008's conceptual design meeting, who pushed for an LCD display on the remote and how was it settled? In the final meeting, what did the component information say a display would need, and which chip did the team choose?
results.gold_answer: The Industrial Designer (Speaker C) pushed for an LCD (programme info, a trendy colour LCD). The PM (Speaker A) opposed it because it did not fit the sturdy, simple design and the docking station was already the special feature; D raised cost and fragility and B called it too much. A concluded 'we skip the LCD display'. In the final meeting the component information said a display requires an advanced chip, so with no display the team chose the simple chip.
results.answer: In the conceptual design meeting (TS3008c), Speaker C (Industrial Designer) pushed hardest for a small LCD display on the remote, arguing it could show programme information, while Speaker B (User Interface Designer) had also raised new display-related functions. Speaker A (Project Manager) objected that it was vulnerable and did not fit the simple, sturdy concept, and the team settled on skipping the LCD, with B and D agreeing. In the final detailed design meeting (TS3008d), the component information said a display requires an advanced chip, but the team chose the simple chip, bringing the component cost to about 12.50 EUR.

results.question: Team TS3008 adopted a base/docking station in its functional design meeting. Who proposed it and what was it for, and what happened to it in the final costing meeting?
results.gold_answer: In meeting b the Marketing Expert (Speaker D) proposed a base with a button that makes a lost remote beep (about 50% of users often lose their remote), and the PM (A) added making it rechargeable; in meeting c the PM called the docking station 'our killer feature'. In the final costing the docking station was not on the cost sheet. With one battery and a simple chip about 2.30 Euro of the 12.50 budget was left. D and B argued a docking station could be built for that, but the PM thought it unrealistic and suggested forgetting it (pushing kinetic power instead, which was not adopted), so the final concept had no docking station.
results.answer: The base/docking station was not clearly adopted in the functional design meeting (TS3008b): Speaker A (Project Manager) proposed a stand-up base on the television so the remote could always be found and stay charged, and it was left open pending production costs. In the final costing meeting (TS3008d) it was judged too expensive, since Speaker A said it would cost about a fifth of the remote's price, and Speaker A then suggested dropping it in favour of a kinetic remote; the group left it unresolved and it did not appear in the final cost list.
